lesson.title: When One Gene Silences Another: Epistasis in Coat Color
lesson.summary: Epistasis occurs when the alleles at one gene mask or override the phenotypic effect of a different gene entirely, which can bend the familiar 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio into a new pattern.
lesson.body:
The dihybrid cross chapter's 9:3:3:1 ratio assumes the two genes involved act completely independently in how they build the final phenotype, each gene contributing its own separate, visible piece of the picture. Epistasis is what happens when that assumption breaks down: the genotype at one gene can determine whether a second gene's effect is even visible at all, rather than the two genes simply adding their effects side by side.

Coat color in mice is a classic worked example. One gene, C, controls whether any pigment is produced in the first place. The dominant C allele allows pigment production to proceed, while the homozygous recessive genotype, cc, blocks pigment production entirely, producing an albino mouse no matter what is happening at any other coat color gene. A separate gene, A, controls the pattern of that pigment whenever pigment is actually being produced: dominant A produces agouti, a banded fur pattern, while homozygous recessive aa produces solid black fur. Gene C is epistatic to gene A because C's genotype can completely hide whatever A is doing.

Working through the cross AaCc by AaCc uses the exact same gamete math as any dihybrid cross, so the underlying genotype ratio comes out as the familiar 9 A_C_ to 3 A_cc to 3 aaC_ to 1 aacc. But at the level of visible phenotype, the A_cc class and the aacc class look identical, both are albino, because cc blocks pigment regardless of what allele is present at the A gene. Combining those two classes turns the underlying 9:3:3:1 genotype ratio into a modified 9:3:4 phenotype ratio: 9 agouti, 3 solid black, and 4 albino.

The key distinction to hold onto is that epistasis is an interaction between two different genes, not a new kind of interaction between two alleles of the same gene the way incomplete dominance and codominance are. It is a useful reminder that a visible phenotype is often the product of an entire pathway of genes working in sequence, where an early step, such as whether pigment is made at all, can completely determine whether a later step's contribution ever becomes visible.
